channel.title: MoveWell
channel.description: Evidence-based exercise guides for every age and ability — gym, yoga, home training and mobility. Clear instructions, real programming, and safety first.

item.title: How to Start Working Out Again (Without Quitting in Week Three)
item.description: Most people who restart exercise quit within a month, and it is rarely a willpower problem. Here is the evidence-based way to structure the first eight weeks so that week five is easier than week one.

item.title: Goblet Squat: The Complete Beginner's Guide
item.description: The best first squat variation for beginners: how to hold the bell, how deep to go, and the three fixes for every common fault.

item.title: Your First Week at the Gym: A Survival Guide
item.description: The gym is not complicated, it is just unfamiliar. A practical guide to your first week: what to bring, how to structure a session, and the unwritten rules that make you look like you belong.

item.title: Push-Up Progressions From Zero to Twenty
item.description: A four-step progression from wall push-ups to full reps, with the hand position, elbow path and core cues that make the difference.

item.title: Why Strength Training After 50 Is Not Optional
item.description: Adults lose roughly 3–8% of muscle mass per decade after 30, accelerating after 60. Strength training slows and partly reverses it. Here is what the evidence says and how to start at 50, 60 or 70.

item.title: Deadlift Technique: Set-Up to Lockout
item.description: A complete deadlift set-up: bar position, hip height, bracing and the pull. Plus when to use a trap bar instead.

item.title: Yoga for People Who Think They Hate Yoga
item.description: If your only experience of yoga was a crowded room, a fast flow and no idea what to do with your arms, the problem was the class, not you. Here is how to find a version that fits.

item.title: A 15-Minute Morning Yoga Flow
item.description: A gentle sequence that moves every major joint, wakes up your spine and takes fifteen minutes — no flexibility required.

item.title: HIIT vs Steady Cardio: What the Research Says
item.description: HIIT is time-efficient; steady cardio is recoverable. The evidence suggests most people should do far more easy cardio and far less HIIT than they currently do. Here is how to split your week.

item.title: Chair Yoga and Balance for Older Adults
item.description: A safe, supported chair-based practice that builds the balance and leg strength behind fewer falls — no floor work required.

item.title: Recovery Is Training: Sleep, Rest Days and Deloads
item.description: Training is the stimulus; recovery is where adaptation happens. What actually matters — sleep, protein, rest days and when to take a deload week — and what is mostly marketing.

item.title: The 20-Minute No-Equipment Home Circuit
item.description: Four movements, five rounds, twenty minutes. A full-body session that works in a living room and scales from beginner to advanced.

item.title: Dead Bug: Core Stability Done Right
item.description: A spine-safe core exercise that trains the deep abdominals to hold position — the skill that protects your back under load.

item.title: HIIT for Beginners: Intervals That Don't Wreck You
item.description: A 20-minute interval session with a low-impact option, plus honest guidance on how often to do HIIT and when to stop.

item.title: Zone 2 Cardio: The Boring Training That Works
item.description: What zone 2 actually means, how to find it without a lab test, and how much easy cardio you need for a bigger engine.

item.title: The 10-Minute Daily Mobility Routine
item.description: Eight movements covering ankles, hips, spine and shoulders — the joints that stiffen from sitting, in ten minutes flat.

item.title: Desk Breaks: 5 Minutes Every Hour
item.description: Six movements you can do in office clothes, no mat and no sweat, that reverse the stiffness of a long sitting day.

item.title: Movement Games for Kids Aged 5–12
item.description: Play-based exercise for children: coordination, balance and strength, disguised as eight games that need no equipment.

item.title: Strength Training After 60: The Four Movements
item.description: Squat, hinge, push and pull with safe starting loads and simple progressions — the four movements that preserve independence.
